figures.cap: building, window and car with 40 degree angle of depression

parts.latex:
The angle of depression from a window to a car on the ground is $40^\circ$.

The car is 50 metres from the base of the building.

\exfigure{719_q10_1}

How high above the ground is the base of the window, correct to the nearest metre?

solutions.latex:
The horizontal dashed line is parallel to the ground, so the angle of elevation from the car to the window is also $40^\circ$ (alternate angles).

In the right-angled triangle, the side opposite $40^\circ$ is the height $h$ and the adjacent side is $50$ m, so use $\tan$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 40^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{50} \\ h &= 50\tan 40^\circ \\ &\approx 41.95 \\ &\approx 42 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

719_q10_1.notes: Brick wall with window, dashed horizontal, sight line to the car, 40° arc with a filled arrowhead, a right-angle mark, the 50 m dimension line (dashed, filled heads, end bars, gap left for the label), NOT TO SCALE and Car. Positions measured from the crop. What is left in the overlay is the spacing of the brick courses in the lower wall and the simplified car outline; all lines, the arc and labels sit in place. Rules 1, 2, 3, 4, 6a, 11.

6162.stem:
Robert walks 5.59 km from his house to the shop on a bearing of 063°. He then turns on a bearing of 124° to walk to the post office, where he is 13.34 km from home.

\exfigure{719_q22_1}

figures.cap: bearing diagram House, Shop, Post office
solution sketch: bearing diagram annotated with angles x, y, 56 degrees, 27 degrees

parts.latex: Find the true bearing of Robert’s house from the post office.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{719_q22_s1}

Let $x$ and $y$ be the angles at $S$ on either side of the north line through $S$, so $\angle HSP = x + y$.
$$y = 180 - 124 = 56^\circ$$
$$x = 63^\circ \quad (\text{alternate angles, parallel north lines})$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle HSP &= 56 + 63 \\ &= 119^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Source drawing kept.

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule in triangle $HSP$, with $Z = \angle HPS$:
$$\dfrac{\sin Z}{5.59} = \dfrac{\sin 119^\circ}{13.34}$$
$$\begin{aligned} Z &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5.59 \sin 119^\circ}{13.34}\right) \\ &= 21.49\ldots \\ &\approx 21^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } H \text{ from } P &= 360 - (56 + 21) \\ &= 283^\circ\text{T} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the sine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

719_q22_1.notes: Bearing diagram: dashed north lines with filled arrowheads, and bearing arcs with arrowheads (63° at H, 124° at S, the reflex bearing at P ending on PH). 5.59 km and 13.34 km are rotated along their sides. Small differences in label position remain (scan font vs house font). Rules 3, 4, 11, 22.

719_q22_s1.notes: Same bearing diagram, with the solution's angles marked as true arcs. The north line at S is extended (dashed) to the south, with x between SH and south and y between south and SP, as in the solution (x = 63 by alternate angles, y = 180 - 124 = 56). Also marked: 56° at P between north and PS, Z at P between PS and PH, and the reflex bearing at P. The teacher wrote x and y above S, which contradicts the solution, so the solution is followed (rule 18). Left out as working marks (rule 17): the green horizontal line, right-angle mark and arrow, the '90-63 = 27°' note, and the 'y = 180-124 = 56°' working. That is why the original score is 0.48; all printed geometry matches. Rules 17, 18, 22.

figures.cap: triangle ABC with sides AC=6, AB=7, BC=8

parts.latex:
What is the smallest angle in the following triangle?

\exfigure{1247_q8_1}

solutions.latex:
In a triangle, the smallest angle is opposite the shortest side.

The sides are $AB=7$, $BC=8$ and $AC=6$, so the shortest side is $AC=6$.

The angle opposite $AC$ is $\angle B$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the smallest angle is } B$$

meta.generated_note: MCQ working written for key B.

1247_q8_1.notes: Triangle ABC with side labels 6, 8, 7 centred beside their sides. The point labels are in maths italic instead of the crop's bold sans-serif (rules 1, 6a, 19).

6359.stem:
The diagram below shows the results of a compass radial survey of a triangular area of land.

\exfigure{1247_q30_1}

figures.cap: compass radial survey: OA=37 m at 300°, OB=43 m at 078°, OC=32 m at 171°
solution sketch: radial survey diagram annotated with angle 138° and side AB

parts.latex: Calculate the distance of $AB$ to the nearest 2 decimal places.
Find the true bearing of $B$ from $A$ to the nearest degree.

criteria: Uses the correct angle ($138^\circ$), or equivalent merit
Applies the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the sine rule,
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{43}=\dfrac{\sin 138^\circ}{74.72}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \theta &= \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{43\sin 138^\circ}{74.72}\right) \\ &= 22^\circ 39' \end{aligned}$$
Using co-interior angles, the bearing is
$$120^\circ-22^\circ39'\approx 097^\circ\text{T}$$
criteria: Correct answer in true bearing form
Uses co-interior angles, or equivalent merit
Applies the sine rule, or equivalent merit

Labels A 300°, B 078°, C 171°, 37 m, 43 m, 32 m, O and NOT TO SCALE are at the crop positions in Times. The original score is lower only because the scan's text is bolder. Rules 1,2,3,11.

figures.cap: triangle of towns T1, T2, T3 with north line
solution sketch: bearing diagram annotated with angles 150, 30, 20 and theta

parts.latex:
The distance between towns $T_1$ and $T_2$ is 35 km and the distance between towns $T_2$ and $T_3$ is 40 km. as shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{717_q41_1}

The bearings of town $T_3$ from town $T_1$ is $150^\circ$ and the bearing of town $T_2$ from town $T_3$ is $020^\circ$.

What is the bearing of town $T_2$ from town $T_1$ to the nearest degree?

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{717_q41_s1}

Using the sine rule in $\triangle T_1T_2T_3$, with $\theta=\angle T_2T_1T_3$:
$$\dfrac{\sin\theta}{40}=\dfrac{\sin 50^\circ}{35}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sin\theta &= \dfrac{40\sin 50^\circ}{35} \\ \theta &\approx 61^\circ \end{aligned}$$
The bearing of $T_2$ from $T_1$ is
$$150^\circ-61^\circ=089^\circ$$
criteria: Sets up the sine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Kept source \exfigure. Rubric written by us.

717_q41_1.notes: Triangle T1T2T3 with a dashed north line through T1 (house aux dashes, filled arrowhead). Labels '35 km', '40 km' and 'DIAGRAM NOT TO SCALE' at the crop positions. The not-to-scale geometry is kept as in the crop (rules 1, 3, 4).

figures.cap: solution sketch: diagram of Lachlan, eagle and nest

parts.latex:
Lachlan is at a lookout. He looks up and sees a white-bellied sea eagle.

The distance from Lachlan to the eagle is 153 metres and it is at an angle of elevation of $63^\circ$.

Lachlan looks down and sees the eagle's nest. The distance from Lachlan to the nest is 87 metres and it is at an angle of depression of $27^\circ$.

Calculate the distance of the eagle from its nest. Answer correct to the nearest metre.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1266_q22_s1}

The angles at Lachlan add to a right angle.
$$63^\circ + 27^\circ = 90^\circ$$
Hence the triangle is right angled, and by Pythagoras' theorem
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \sqrt{153^2 + 87^2} \\ &\approx 176 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds that the triangle is right angled, or equivalent merit
Sketches a diagram correctly showing all information, or equivalent merit

1266_q22_s1.notes: Sketch of Lachlan, the eagle and the nest, with a fine dashed horizontal through Lachlan using the house aux dash. Labels are 153 m, 87 m, 63° and 27°. The sketch's proportions are kept (rule 1: not drawn to true angles). The crop has no angle arcs, so none were added. Round 2 moved the nest vertex and the labels to the measured positions.
